storyboard.claim: The episode opens on the book's first question: whose task was that — yours or your father's disappointment?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two labelled buckets, YOURS and YOUR FATHER'S DISAPPOINTMENT, while the young man stands burdened beside them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cold open: the video starts on the separation-of-tasks question itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns a rhetorical question into a visible either/or, so a mute viewer sees the split before any explanation.

storyboard.claim: The heavy backpack of expectations you have carried your whole life is not actually yours.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A boulder crushing the young man's shoulders — the 'backpack of expectations' made literal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the opening question: this is the load being asked about.
storyboard.addedInformation: The boulder gives the invisible burden real weight; the narration only calls it a backpack.

storyboard.claim: Nobody forced the burden on you — you volunteered to put it on.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A surprised reaction shot of the young man as the narrator says he chose the load himself.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the weight itself to its origin: you put it on.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the startled face carries the vertigo of the realization; the choice itself stays in the words.

storyboard.claim: This deep dive targets a text that quietly then loudly became a massive global phenomenon.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher introducing the topic straight to camera, no icon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the personal hook to the subject of the episode.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: a talking head plus the callout; the scale of the phenomenon lives only in the text.

storyboard.claim: The book is The Courage to Be Disliked by Ichiro Kishimi and Fumitake Koga.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher holding up the book itself — the episode's title object.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the phenomenon introduced in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the exact title on screen while the narrator gives the authors, and the book prop fixes the object of study.

storyboard.claim: This is not your typical soft, feel-good self-help book — it is a radical, almost aggressive translation of Adler's theories.
storyboard.concreteVisual: No cozy book imagery at all: the philosopher speaking straight, while the screen carries only the counter-description.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Immediately corrects the expectation the title just created.
storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the contrast instead of the negation — nothing soft appears on screen, so the picture never says the wrong thing.

storyboard.claim: The book is a radical translation of the theories of Alfred Adler, a 20th-century Austrian psychiatrist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler himself in period dress — the thinker behind the book, making his first appearance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From what the book is not to whose thinking it delivers.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the spoken name a face and introduces the only historical figure in the cast.

storyboard.claim: The first titan everyone instantly names in early psychology is Sigmund Freud.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher counting off the first name to camera; Freud's name on screen, no portrait.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the establishment figure Adler will be measured against.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: only the name and its spelling are carried; the picture adds the host's emphasis.

storyboard.claim: Alfred Adler is widely considered the third giant of that exact same era, right there with Freud and Jung.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler with a trophy — standing status among the period's giants.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Freud and Jung to the man this episode is really about.
storyboard.addedInformation: The trophy turns 'giant' into visible status; the callout supplies the ranking the icon cannot.

storyboard.claim: Adler was a core foundational member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society alongside Freud.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A city icon for Vienna with Adler standing as its member.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From his rank beside Freud to his actual seat inside the society.
storyboard.addedInformation: The city gives the society a place, so the membership is not a floating name.

storyboard.claim: Adler stayed in the society until he and Freud split fundamentally and catastrophically over how human beings operate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A war icon for the scale of the break, Adler walking away from it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From founding membership to the rupture that ended it.
storyboard.addedInformation: The war icon reads instantly as a big fight, and staging only Adler walking keeps the two men from looking identical.

callout.text: Freud and Jung became household names

storyboard.claim: While Freud and Jung became household names whose terms are embedded in our daily language.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher naming their fame to camera — no portraits, no icons.
storyboard.onScreenText: Freud and Jung became household names
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the split with who emerged famous from it.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the phrase alone carries their fame; the picture adds only emphasis.

storyboard.claim: Adler's theory quietly permeated the culture while he himself never got the marquee credit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler slumped and uncredited as 'the marquee credit' is struck through above him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly answers the last beat: the others got the fame, Adler did not.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike shows a credit withheld, and his deflated posture keeps the beat from reading as praise.

storyboard.claim: Kishimi and Koga do not present Adler's ideas through some dry academic textbook.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher speaking while 'dry academic textbook' is crossed out — deliberately no textbook on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Adler's obscurity to how this particular book chooses to deliver him.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike carries the negation; drawing a textbook plainly would have said the opposite.

storyboard.claim: The book is written as a Socratic dialogue — a literal continuous conversation between two characters, led by an endlessly patient philosopher.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-shot of the philosopher and the youth facing each other mid-conversation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Replaces the rejected textbook with the book's actual form.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the structure instead of naming it: two opposed people are the whole text.

storyboard.claim: Opposite him is a cynical, deeply insecure young man the book refers to simply as the youth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man introduced alone, slouched with his guard up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the second voice of the dialogue just described.
storyboard.addedInformation: His posture performs the insecurity the narrator only states.

storyboard.claim: The youth thinks the world is a chaotic, miserable mass of contradictions, hates himself and society, and storms into the philosopher's study to prove the old man wrong.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth jabbing a finger at the unmoving philosopher.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From who the youth is to what he does in the opening scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: The attack pose shows the confrontation the narration only describes as 'storms in'.

storyboard.claim: The youth acts as a stand-in for every single doubt the reader might have.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A mirror — the young man studying his own reflection, the reader seeing themselves in him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the structural job of the character just introduced.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mirror makes 'stand-in for you' literal, which the narration never says outright as an image.

storyboard.claim: When the philosopher makes outrageous, counterintuitive claims, the youth yells at him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth mid-shout with a raised finger while the philosopher stays calm.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the reader's doubts into open combat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The yelling-versus-calm staging is the book's engine, readable without a word of audio.

storyboard.claim: He pushes back hard, even calling the philosopher's argument dangerous academic sophistry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth leaning in with the accusation while the philosopher listens, unbothered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the sharpest charge the youth levels in the exchange.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the exact insult on screen so the stakes of the argument survive muting.

callout.text: the philosopher holds all the cards

storyboard.claim: Analysed honestly, the dialogue is essentially a staged, rigged trial where the philosopher holds all the cards.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A law icon for the courtroom framing, the philosopher gesturing like a man who already has the verdict.
storyboard.onScreenText: the philosopher holds all the cards
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Steps back from the fight to judge the structure of the whole text.
storyboard.addedInformation: The law icon makes 'trial' literal; the callout carries 'rigged', which no icon can honestly draw.

storyboard.claim: The youth never actually wins a single round in the debate — it is a rigged game.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A game icon over the defeated youth: the contest was fixed before it started.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Restates the trial verdict in the narrator's blunter words.
storyboard.addedInformation: Icon plus slumped loser shows the fix even to a viewer with the sound off.

storyboard.claim: Watching the trap snap shut around the youth's arguments is mesmerizing, and it leads into the episode's core thesis.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher making a closing gesture as the youth's objection is dismantled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the rigged structure into the reason we keep watching.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon reads 'trap' literally, so the closing gesture and the callout carry the metaphor.

storyboard.claim: The book is famous for its highly controversial attack on the concept of trauma.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sword — the attack itself, aimed at the phrase on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the thesis the previous beat promised.
storyboard.addedInformation: The weapon makes 'attack' visible while the callout states exactly what is being attacked.

storyboard.claim: People get very heated about this attack on trauma on social media.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An insert on a phone in the young man's hands — the feed where the arguments flare up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the book's claim to the public reaction it triggers.
storyboard.addedInformation: The smartphone grounds a modern controversy in a place every viewer recognizes.

storyboard.claim: The attack on trauma is only the shiny provocative object — the marketing hook that gets you in the door and gets you defensive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A door — the entrance the provocation is designed to open.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the heated reaction of the last beat as marketing, not argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door turns the idiom into a picture: the controversy is a way in.

storyboard.claim: The real engine of the book — the mechanism that makes everything else work — is a concept Adler calls the separation of tasks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler holding up a lightbulb: the concept he is naming.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the hook to the machinery underneath it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Adler on screen with his own idea marks it as the book's core rather than its marketing.

storyboard.claim: Most of what you are carrying right now is someone else's expectation, and the title's courage is simply the courage to hand those expectations back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The boulder from the opening returns — the weight that turns out to belong to other people.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Defines what the separation of tasks actually separates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reusing the cold-open boulder ties the core concept back to the burden the viewer was shown first.

callout.text: demolish the house you live in

storyboard.claim: Before that engine can run, the book has to demolish the house you are currently living in and clear the foundation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A home icon — the house you are currently living in, the worldview up for demolition.
storyboard.onScreenText: demolish the house you live in
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the engine to the demolition work required before it can run.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the metaphor drawable; the words clarify the house is a belief system, not a building.

storyboard.claim: That demolition begins with a massive, unapologetic fight with Freud, staged inside the philosopher's study.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A war icon for the scale of the clash, now dropped into the study scene.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the opponent and moves the episode from essay into scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: The set change marks the shift into the book's dialogue; the war icon shows a battle, not a lecture.

callout.text: a friend shut in his room

storyboard.claim: In the study the youth sits slouched with his arms crossed, totally defensive, telling the philosopher about a friend who has shut himself in his room for years.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth sunk in a chair with his arms crossed, talking; the philosopher opposite him.
storyboard.onScreenText: a friend shut in his room
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the frame of the fight to the case the youth opens with.
storyboard.addedInformation: His posture matches the narration exactly, and the friend stays off screen so the story can build.

callout.text: one single step outside his house

storyboard.claim: If that friend tries to take even one single step outside his house, he suffers violent palpitations.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A door — the threshold the friend cannot cross without his body rebelling.
storyboard.onScreenText: one single step outside his house
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms from years shut in to the moment of attempted exit.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the phobia at a specific, visible place; the symptom itself stays in the narration.

storyboard.claim: The youth reads the symptom as undeniable proof: past trauma dictates our present reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step chain, PAST TRAUMA -> PRESENT REALITY, while the youth makes the case to the philosopher.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the friend's symptom into the argument built on top of it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Draws the causal arrow the narrator only speaks, so the model is visible before it is named.

storyboard.claim: Something terrible in childhood leaving him permanently broken is the classic cause and effect model we all intuitively accept.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth spelling out the model; the philosopher listening without conceding.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the chain from the previous beat its name.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the diagram already drew the chain; this beat only supplies its label.

storyboard.claim: Freud called this model etiology: the present effect is strictly determined by occurrences in the past — a psychic wound from childhood causes present unhappiness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher naming the term to camera — no icon, since etiology has no literal picture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the model's shape to its technical name.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: a talking beat; the callout is the only place the term exists on screen.

storyboard.claim: We have embraced that linear narrative as a culture — we love a good origin story — until Adler drops a bomb on the youth's worldview.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler stepping forward as the narrator announces the bomb about to hit that worldview.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the accepted model to the challenger about to break it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the disruptor on screen before he acts, so the next beat lands as his move.

storyboard.claim: Adler entirely rejects etiology and champions something called teleology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler waving the old model aside, the highlighted phrase carrying both the rejection and the replacement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the bomb promised in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The dismissive gesture keeps the negation visible without drawing the rejected model as true.

storyboard.claim: The youth demands to know how teleology applies to the shut-in friend who is literally shaking at the door.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The youth pressing the objection, unconvinced, while the philosopher prepares to answer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Forces the new term back onto the concrete case from the study.
storyboard.addedInformation: Keeps the challenge visible: a theory is being tested against a body that really shakes.

storyboard.claim: Teleology is the study of the purpose of a given phenomenon rather than its historical cause — and the friend's physiological response is still real.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A target — purpose as the thing the behaviour is aimed at — beside the explaining philosopher.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the youth's demand with the definition of teleology.
storyboard.addedInformation: The target gives 'purpose' a literal image, and the claim records that the symptom itself is still accepted as real.

storyboard.claim: Adler argues that we do not break because of our past — we are not fragile machines where a broken gear in 1995 causes a malfunction now.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler rejecting the machine metaphor outright — no broken machine is ever shown as fact.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the purpose-first definition to the deepest claim about human durability.
storyboard.addedInformation: The claim lands as a clean reversal of the model the video spent the last beats building.
